speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, will the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) advise the house if he

Privilege-Mr. Spotlon

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
subtopic: TEST SHIPMENTS OF GRAIN THROUGH CHURCHILL THIS SEASON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have received no requests from anyotie in western Canada for space in this trial shipment. No one has communicated with me except the On-to-the-Bay Association, who stated that they had disposal of 150,000 bushels, which would comprise about half a cargo. While on my feet may I add that statements have appeared in the papers that Mr. Dunning had said repeatedly that if his party were returned to power they would ship 5,000,000 bushels this fall. A search has been made of the records and of Hansard and no such statement has been found. I do not believe Mr. Dunning ever made any such statement. I ask these western papers either to tell me the source of their information or to stop misquoting and misrepresenting.
On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of personal privilege. The Toronto Daily Star of Monday, July 27, contains the following headline:
M.P. Franks Circular Soliciting Students for Business College.
Had Several Hundred Mimeographed in House, George Spotton admits.
The article itself reads as follows:
Enclosed in an official envelope of the House of Commons, Ottawa, a letter written on government stationery received by a Toronto girl, carries a mime'ographed text of about 250 words soliciting her patronage for the Canada Business College, an organization owned and operated by George Spotton, Conservative M.P. for Huron North.
The letter is signed "Canada Business College, per George Spotton, M.P. for North Huron." The outside envelope is franked for free postage, and on the back in large type is the word "free."
Also enclosed is a return envelope, on House of Commons stationery, addressed to G. Mc-Eacbren, B.A., Canada Business College, 274 College Street, Toronto, Ontario.
Interviewed by The Star in Toronto to-day, Mr. Spotton admitted that the letter was one sent out by him.
"How many have you sent out?" The Star asked. "Several hundred," Mr. Spotton said. "Where were they mimeographed?" "In the house. They were dictated to a government stenographer and passed through the usual
channels. All letters dispatched by members have to be authorized by the chief of stenographers and the Clerk of the House."
"Were these letters authorized?" "They were authorized. In fact it was Mr. Smith, head stenographer, who suggested that they should be multigraphed to save time. Otherwise I could have had carbon copies made."
"Do you consider this method of writing business letters quite in order?" "Certainly. I consider it one of my perquisites. Every public office has perquisites. If a man were not allowed to keep in touch with his business while in Ottawa, except by hiring his own stenographer, then a parliamentary career would be for rich men only."
"Is this a general practice?" "Even more so than in my case.' Mr. Smith told me a short time ago that I had been particularly lenient in the use of his stenographers this session. I am not trying 'to put it over.' Both Mr. Smith and the clerk have long experience in parliamentary custom."
Mr. Spotton stated he did not think that the matter would be brought up in the house. "It was done before and it came out that the persons who protested had been themselves making particularly free use of departmental facilities," he said. "If anyone thinks they will do me harm in my constituency, I will say that my electors would laugh if anyone brings up the question in the house, of my having saved $17 or $18 or $21 by using the house stenographers, stationery and stamps. Every envelope bears my initial, written either by me or by someone else on my behalf. That means that I am responsible for that letter."
I wish to say that the Toronto Daily Star was particularly fair to me. During the week end they searched for me all over western Ontario and sought an interview before they published this item.

Will the hon. member
state bis question of privilege? He has laid the ground therefor by reading the article, but it is not in order to make a speech.

The following appears
under date of Ottawa, July 27:
"Offhand, I should say such a practice would be an abuse of the franking privileges," an official of the Post Office Department told The Star, commenting on Mr. Spotton's circular.
That is my chief complaint. I will read another paragraph in the article, as follows: The regulations governing franking are quite broad and indefinite, the text reading merely as follows: "letters and other mailable matter sent to or by any member of the Senate or House of Commons are carried free of postage." No limitation as to the character of the letter is contained in the regulations.

Will the hon. member
state his question of privilege?

I deny absolutely the
accusation contained in the heading of this article. A cursory reading of the article would make it appear that the hon. member for
Customs Tariff

North Huron was abusing his privileges. I ask that the Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) give the name of the post office official who says that a member of this honourable body has abused his franking privileges. I state: This is not correct. A lawyer in the house fills out his deeds, leases and mortgages and keeps in touch with his clients, so does the manufacturer, and if a humible business college manager cannot keep in touch with his business, then he cannot remain in the house.
The hon. gentleman can direct his complaint to the Post Office Department which, and not this house, controls the franking privilege.

Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Minister of Finance) moved the third reading of Bill No. Ill, to amend the customs tariff.
He said: The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) said that on the third reading he desired to move an amendment and the matter stood over to afford him that opportunity.

I am not going to discuss my amendment at any length, because it has been discussed on several previous occasions, and I think we have exhausted all the discussion on that particular subject. I am not, however, so sure that I am really responsible for the amendment I have to offer. I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is responsible for it; in fact, I think the Conservative party is responsible for it, because in 1930 they advocated an amendment to the customs tariff, and taking my cue from their position I consider that industries which are receiving benefits from the customs tariff should be prepared at least to give their workingmen protection in accordance with the treaty of Versailles. My amendment is along the lines of the one I moved when the bill was last in committee. I beg to move:
That the bill be not now read a third time but be referred back to the committee empowering the committee to add the following section:
The governor in council may direct from time to time that any industry, the products of which receive protection under this act, shall demonstrate to the satisfaction of the governor in council that freedom of association for employees for all lawful purposes is permitted in the operation of such industry, and that the hours of labour and rates of wages are observed consistent with the provisions of the labour part of the treaty of Versailles concluded at Paris, France, on June 28, 1919.

Will those in favour of
the amendment kindly say aye?
Aye.
Mr. Speaker-
Will those opposed to the amendment kindly say nay?
Nay.
I declare the amendment lost.

Mr. Speaker, I was on my feet before you put the motion, trying to catch your eye or ear. Some of us are seated at a long distance from the Speaker, and when we stand in our places in regard to a matter of this kind, I think we have a right to be heard before a motion is put. I was standing in my place before Your Honour put the motion.

The hon. member for
Winnipeg North Centre rose while I was putting the question. He was too late. The question is now on the motion for the third reading of the bill. If the hon. member desires to speak on that, not having done so before, that is his privilege.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
I do not propose to discuss
at any length the proposal put forward by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan). It seems to me that this is quite in keeping with the suggestion as made last year by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). I think it was read once before, but I want to read once again what he said on May 21, 1930. He said:
Did Canada sign the treaty of peace? Did Canada thereby become, amongst the nations of the world, a member of the League of Nations? The answer is yes. Did the Liberal party, in solemn convention assembled, adopt the Labour articles of the treaty of peace? The answer is yes. Did the Conservative party do the same? The answer is yes. To-night the question is whether or not the parliament of the Dominion of Canada that signed the treaty of peace, with two great parties pledging themselves to its observance and the group to my left also supporting it, is helpless. It is true that property and civil rights are matters exclusively under the control of the provincial legislatures. It is equally true that this parliament may, if it so pleases, impose conditions with respect to any matter wherein it expends public money or confers a benefit or privilege upon any person or class or corporation.
I do not think the case could have been better put. Since only yesterday the Prime Minister definitely assured us t-hat he was prepared to carry out the pledges made by the people who elected him to his present position, I can scarcely understand-

Carried.

Customs Act
. Mr. SPENCER:	Can we not have order
in tfhis chamber ?

I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that since it was only yesterday the Prime Minister told us that since he had been elected by the convention at Winnipeg to the position of leader of the Conservative party he was prepared to stand 'by the program laid down at that time, I can scarcely understand his position in this matter. Today I find that he is taking no steps whatever to carry out the solemn pledges adopted at that convention, and which he himself stated so well only a year ago when leader of the opposition. I can say no more than that.

speechtext: I understand that the government still believes in the principle of the bill, but for some special reason cannot proceed with it at this session.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOSS OR RENUNCIATION OF CANADIAN NATIONALITY
speechtext:
I think I explained the
other day to the hon. member for St. James that because the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Gordon) had been employed on a select committee of the house it had been impossible to secure agreements between the Department of Immigration and Colonization, the Department of External Affairs and the Department of the Secretary of State with respect to certain necessary amendments to the Immigration Act which would be required to comply with the terms of this measure. subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT

speechtext: Hon. E. B. RYCKMAN (Minister of National Revenue) moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendment made by the Senate to Bill No. 39, to amend the Customs Act.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext: What is the nature of the amendment?

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The amendment is
really formal in character, and is quite acceptable. If this bill as amended in the Senate becomes law, we will still have in our law subsection 7 of section 151 as it stands at present, although it is understood we will not exercise jurisdiction beyond the three-mile limit pending appeal to the privy council in the Dunphy vs. Croft case. Then, if a favourable decision is obtained from the privy council, a proclamation would be issued, the effect of which would be to repeal subsection 7 as it now stands and substitute therefor the new subsection 7 as proposed in our original bill.
Motion agreed to; amendment read the second time and concurred in.

I think the Prime Minister misunderstood me, Mr. Chairman, I did not offer it as an amendment. I think this is a measure that we can very well deal with without offering amendments from our side. What I had in mind I would rather offer as a suggestion.
The question of the amendment of the Old Age Pensions Act has been fairly well discussed in this house during this session, and I am not going to cover the ground further. The leader of the opposition has suggested that the government Should take over the old age pensions scheme and administer
it with the Dominion paying 100 per cent, and my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has offered a suggestion with regard to the inclusion of the blind. I should like to say to the Prime Minister, in case he does not know it, that I think I am safe in saying five of the provinces have signified their willingness, either directly or indirectly, to have the blind taken in when the Old Age Pensions Act is amended.
The amendment I suggest to the Prime Minister at this time has to do with a matter which is causing a great deal of hardship. It is true that only a very few people are affected, but still those few should be entitled to a pension which, because of the way the act reads at present, they cannot get. As I said before, when we first introduced this measure we did not know how many provinces would take up the scheme, and naturally it was desired to protect the provinces who first took part, so that if only one or two provinces participated they would be protected from an influx of old people from other provinces. So we included subsection (d) of section 8, which reads:
(d) has resided in the province in which the application for pension is made for the five years immediately preceding the said date;
We find, in the administration of the act, that, I think, fifty old people have resided in one or more of the provinces for more than five years but have not been in any one province for that length of time. They have been in this country all their lives but are unable to obtain a pension. When the interprovincial board met to discuss amendments and new regulations they drafted the following suggested subsection to replace the present subsection (d) of section 8:
(d) has resided in the province in which the application for pension is made, or in that province and in another province with which an agreement under this act is in force, for the five years immediately preceding the said date.
That is to say, if a person had been in this country for twenty years and had resided for five years in one or more of the provinces coming under this scheme, he would be permitted to apply for pension, and since the five provinces under the scheme desire this amendment I suggest to the Prime Minister that he give consideration to it, because after all is said and done it will only affect about fifty persons.

I had not intended to say anything further in committee, and had it not been that at the close of
Old Age Pensions Act

yesterday's sitting my right hon. friend by his remarks rather left the impression that in some way I was seeking to block this legislation, I would not speak at the moment. Hon. members of the committee will see that when the bill came up for second reading I drew the attention of t'he Prime Minister to the fact that the preamble contained a clause which I thought would create some difficulty unless it were removed. I thought it desirable that it should be removed in order to ensure the enactment of the measure. When my right hon. friend rose to speak he said he intended to withdraw that particular clause, and it was withdrawn.
Later I spoke about the desirability of the government taking over the administration of the measure, particularly since it now involved a contribution of 75 per cent on the part of the federal administration; I said it seemed rather anomalous that the body which was paying the largest part of the cost of the scheme should not be the body to administer it. My remarks were all intended to convey the hope that the government would move as rapidly as possible towards the administration of the scheme in its entirety in order completely to relieve the provinces of that responsibility. I also said that in speaking during the last campaign I had expressed the view that it was desirable that there should be a dominion-provincial conference to review as between the dominion and the provinces all these matters of social services and to delimit the fields of taxation and of expenditure and that I thought it would have been of advantage to the dominion had such a conference been held before this legislation was brought in. A conference for that particular purpose might well have taken place previous to this session of parliament. At any rate, it might have been arranged that a conference would take place between now and next year at which time a 100 per cent payment might be agreed upon. My sole contention in that regard was that in making our financial readjustments with the provinces, being trustees of the dominion's purse, we would in such an event be in a stronger position than would be the case if, before holding any conference of the kind, we were committed to further extensions of these and other grants.
Then I think my right hon. friend rather left the impression that in some way, when in office, I had been responsible for beginning the grants in general. May I say that the policy of making grants to the provinces 
started with previous administrations; that they had been made with respect to highways, agricultural instruction, technical education, loans for housing and unemployment relief before the Liberal administration ever came into office. With respect to old age pensions, at the time the Liberal government undertook to pay 50 per cent of the cost it was recognized that it was desirable to have a national scheme, but at that time anything of the sort was impossible owing to well known constitutional difficulties. The government of the day had been advised by the Department of Justice as to its authority and rights and powers in the matter, and as a result of the advice given the government reached the necessary conclusion that unless it were to be made a contributory scheme, which at the time we were not prepared to consider, the federal government could not inaugurate an old age pension scheme in any other way than by grants to the provinces. That was the reason why the government of the day made the grant of 50 per cent; it did so with a view to bringing about throughout Canada a uniform system of old age pensions and also with a view to giving time to remove any constitutional impediment to the dominion taking over the entire scheme. It was felt that the fact that all the provinces would be prepared to accept an old age pension scheme on the lines laid down to secure uniformity would of itself be the strongest evidence that it was desirable to have such a scheme on a national scale, administered federally.
That is the sum and substance of the remarks I made yesterday, and if my right hon. friend felt that in any way they were susceptible of another interpretation I hope he will permit hon. members of the committee to read for themselves the Hansard report.

To assist in the conservation and development of the deep-sea fisheries and the demand for fish, $190,000.

Mr. Chairman, before this item is carried I would like to deal with certain articles which have appeared in the press in connection with the fisheries of Hudson bay. I feel that I would fail miserably in my duty as the representative of that great country if I did not correct some of the statements which have been made.
The Ottawa Journal of April 24 contained an article stating that the government spent a large sum of money last summer making an investigation into the fishing possibilities and that no fidh were taken. That article would cause the average citizen not acquainted with that country to believe that there is no fish in the Hudson bay, and to that statement I take exception, I intend to place on the records of this house certain evidence in regard to the fishing possibilities in that great body of water. This information should be of great benefit to hon. members of the house as well as to the people of Canada generally.
In a book published by the Department of the Interior entitled The Unexploited West, I find the following information in connection with Hudson bay. J. B. Tyrrell, a well known engineer, stated that salmon of the very finest quality are found in abundance both in Hudson bay and the''straits. In another paragraph, Mr. Hanbury of the department states that he has seen Eskimos with cod and fish in great abundance along both the east and west coast of the bay. Mr. Christie, chief inspector of the Hudson's Bay Company, stated before the Senate committee that salmon were found in large numbers at Churchill as soon as the ice cleared out of the river, which was about the middle of June. He stated that they entered the river and went out with the tide, and he thought that these salmon were as large as those he had seen in Scotland. Mr. A. P. Low, director of the Geological Survey of Canada, examined by the Senate committee, stated that the Arctic salmon found on the east and west sides of the bay were very abundant. He stated that this was an excellent fish, beautifully coloured and resembling the western salmon more than it did the Atlantic or eastern salmon. He stated that salmon fishing in Hudson bay would no doubt have a commercial outlet as soon as marketing facili-
Supply-Fisheries

ties were provided. He stated that the whitefish to be found in the bay was a very fine fish.
Captain Bernier, the explorer, published an excellent book entitled Hudson Bay and Straits which book contained a report of the special committee appointed to report on the navigability and fishing resources of Hudson bay and the straits. Captain Bernier states that at the entrance to the straits there is any amount of codfish, and that east of there they used to take from 200 to 300 fish a day with line fishing. He states that he caught a few halibut at Fullerton and some salmon further north. He found every river along the coast teeming with fish, particularly with salmon trout weighing from 10 to IS pounds. In the same bulletin, Mr. J. B. Tyrrell, a mining engineer and explorer who has made several trips into the bay, states that he met an enormous number of walrus which swarmed about the shores of the islands. These walrus live on clams and other shell fish and are to be found in great numbers. He states that they saw many seals and caught large quantities of fish, including salmon, whitefish and sturgeon. He states that seals appear quite frequently along the shores of the straits and bay.
So much for the evidence given before the Senate committee, to which I might add my own knowledge gained during eighteen years spent in this country. I have seen as many as 1,000 whales come into the harbours of Nelson and Churchill at one time. These whales live on fish, so that if what some seal expert who writes for the Ottawa Journal says is true, that there are no fish in the bay, there would not 'be any whales or seals or walruses, because those mammals live exclusively on fish. Inside of an hour using a short net, I have taken out of the bay more salmon than would fill a small boat. Last summer, when I was there during my election campaign trying to capture a few votes from a handpicked bunch of Liberals that were put in there, I saw about 1,000 whales chasing a shoal of herring. It was a great sight and was evidence that there must be fish in the bay.
It is true the government sent a trawler there last year to do some investigating in the deep water. It is also quite true they did not catch any fish by this deep-water trawling. Every schoolboy in that part of the country knows fish are not to be found in the deep water of the bay, because the water there is only one degree above freezing point, but we know there is a great number of fish along the shores and in the estuaries of the rivers. It is interesting to note that the fishing industry of British Columbia produces 
two-fifths of the fishery wealth of the dominion. Exactly the same condition exists in Hudson bay. I cannot too strongly urge upon the minister the necessity of a more thorough investigation of the shoreline and estuary fisheries of Hudson bay. It is of great importance to the Hudson Bay railway and the people of the west that a complete investigation is made. Boats should be sent in there, equipped to ply on the east and west shores of the bay with a good supply of gill nets, small boats and net fishermen. I sincerely hope the minister will provide for that at the earliest possible moment, and that it will be carried out.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Fisheries) :
speechtext:
If the hon. member for Nelson reads the report outlining the result of the investigation into the fisheries of Hudson bay, I think he will see that the statement that there were no fish had reference merely to what is known as deepssea fish, that is, cod, halibut and fish of that type. There is no question that the results of the experiments conducted by the Loubyrne demonstrate that fact. It is well known, that for many years there have been rich cod fisheries in Hudson strait, especially at the entrance. As a matter of fact, Newfoundland fishermen operated cod fisheries there as far back as a century ago. It is also well known that t'he rivers flowing into Hudson bay are teeming with fish; that those are what we know as freshwater fish. My hon. friend referred to the fact that there were seals and whales in the bay and they would not be there unless there were something on which they could feed. As a matter of fact, I am informed by the officers of my department that shoals of caplin come in there from time to time and they form the most delectable food for seals and whales. We are well satisfied the rivers are teeming with fish that an investigation on the part of the department scarcely seems necessary excepting that I might add that even this year we have issued a number of experimental licences to individuals who are conducting fishing operations there and a condition attached to the licence which was given to them was that they Should report to the department the result of their season's operations. Therefore, to the extent that they succeed, we shall add to the store of knowledge we already have.
In conclusion, I should like to assure my hon. friend we are already seized of the fact that there are rich fisheries in the rivers and tributaries surrounding Hudson bay.

I must say very frankly to the Minister of Fisheries that the northern

Suppl y-Fisheries
seotion of northern Ontario is not satisfied with what I may call the Hachey report. I believe the government should find it possible this year to spend another $65,000 in order to make a very thorough inquiry into the situation, because we maintain that there are deepwater fish in Hudson bay. I am going to give the history of the reasons why such an inquiry was made last year. At page 81 of the sixty-third annual report of the Fisheries branch, I find the following information :
Hudson Bay Resources
A quick trip visit was made to the Churchill at Hudson bay during the late summer, the object being to ascertain what available information there was relative to the fisheries of the bay and the estuaries of the big rivers. A special report was made to the department, in which a recommendation was made to send a properly equipped trawler from the outside to investigate conditions in the deeper areas of the bay.
Along the Manitoba coastline and entering the rivers, there appear to be two important varieties of fish, the Arctic trout and herring or ciscoes. The former centre on the Churchill, while the latter seem more plentiful towards the Nelson, also whitefish although these fish are apparently not very plentiful. There are also to be found indefinite indications of both cod and halibut, but nothing to base a conclusion on whether or not these are indigenous to the waters of the bay.
Again it is clearly stated that in Hudson bay there are deepwater fish. In our section of the country we were all astonished when we read the report which was made after only a few days spent in making investigations over an area which covers 540,000 square miles in Hudson bay and 150,000 square miles in Hudson strait and Ungava bay, and which stated that there were no deepwater fish.
I am going to read the preliminary report of the investigations of the Hudson bay and strait fisheries expedition of 1930. On page one of the report I find the following: Instructions From The Department
The instructions received from the department were in part as follows:
"Actual fishing operations should be begun as soon after Hudson strait is entered as may be deemed feasible, but there should be no unnecessary loss of time to the trawler incurred in the journey to Churchill, or fishing carried on to the extent that might endanger exhaustion of the coal supply before Churchill would be reached. Also fishing should be again conducted in the strait on the homeward journey to as great an extent as conditions will permit."
On page 2, I find the following:
Operations In Hudson Bay
On the journey across Hudson bay the biological, physical and chemical conditions of the waters were investigated. These investigations consisted in,-
(1)	collecting samples for the qualitative and quantitative determination of the smaller organisms present which would form an important link in the food cycle of life in these waters,
(2)	determining the temperature of the water at various depths and localities,
(3)	obtaining samples of water for the determination of the salinity of the water at various depths and localities, and
(4)	setting out drift bottles for the purpose of mapping the prevailing surface water movements.
On page 3 of the report they give the results:
Results
The expedition travelled a total distance of about 8,000 nautical miles. Of this amount 3,100 miles were covered in occupying the various stations for the purposes of the investigation. The total distance was covered in approximately fifty-six days so that the average daily distance travelled was 143 miles.
The record of fishing operations furnishes the particulars of the actual fishing done.
Our objection is to the actual fishing done. We maintain in our district that the time allotted was not sufficient to make a thorough investigation. The report continues:
Hand lines were used at several points for seven hours and fifteen minutes. Drift nets wrere used for twelve hours. Long lines were used for two hours and fifty-five minutes, and trawling operations were carried on for fifty-seven hours and fifty minutes. As a result of the total work covering the whole of Hudson hay not a single commercial fish was taken.
I stated previously that Hudson bay comprises an area of 540,000 square miles. Was it possible to investigate such a large area in such a short time? They also had to investigate fishing conditions in Hudson strait which, including Ungava bay, comprises an area of 150,000 square miles. It was absolutely impossible to make a very good investigation under the circumstances. I must give credit to the officers in charge because they did the best they could in the time allotted, but I repeat that at least a three months' investigation should be conducted in these waters next summer. Anyone will realize that it would take at least three months to make a thorough investigation into the resources of Hudson bay. Quoting from the report, I find this:
In looking over a chart of the Hudson bay region the experienced fisherman would note immediately the absence of anything that would correspond to the various "banks" so familiar and appreciated by the fishermen of the Atlantic Coast. There is one small region in the vicinity of stations 39 and 40 which might be called a bank.
I challenge that statement. Any navigator in those waters knows that there is more than one bank in Hudson bay. The whole of James bay is practically a bank itself, and
Sup pi y-Fishe ries

there are unlimited schools of fish in that section of Hudson bay. They wind up their report by saying:
The scientific investigations were carried on concurrently with the fishing operations, and sufficient data is available for the correct interpretation of the fishing results. The cursory examination of the material collected and the data noted suggest that the waters of Hudson bay are similar to the unproductive waters of much higher latitudes.
Again I challenge that statement. The greater part of Hudson bay is in a temperate zone. The climatic conditions in James bay are identical with climatic conditions in Cochrane or northern Ontario. The statement in the report is not a true statement of the conditions in Hudson bay.
In all sincerity I say that this is not a political question but as a man from northern Ontario I am particularly interested, as all hon. members must realize, in this question which vitally affects the northern sections of Ontario, Quebec and Manitoba. Only a few years ago the Ontario government wanted to extend the government railway northward from North Bay, and some people prominent in public life said that not a single dollar should be spent in that northern country which they said consisted only of stunted poplar and muskeg. To-day that district, which comprises Cobalt, Porcupine and Kirkland Lake, is the treasure house not only of northern Ontario 'but of Canada as a whole. The same is true of Hudson bay. Anyone who looks at the map must be arrested by that great inland sea, and no one will say that not a single deep sea fish could be caught in that vast expanse of water. I know that the minister has at heart the development of the fisheries of this country. There have been rumours that there is fear of competition from Hudson bay with the fisheries of the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts. I do not believe that there is anything in that, but I would point out to the minister that we are fully equipped now to give a thirty-six hour refrigerator car service from Moose Factory to Toronto, and a forty-eight hour refrigerator car service from Moose Factory to New York. So we are highly interested in this problem. In conclusion, I would make a strong appeal to the minister to send a trawler up there this fall, to quarter there for the winter months, and then conduct a three months' inquiry into deep sea fishing in Hudson bay next summer.

I think we are all agreed
with my hon. friend from North Timiskaming that this is not a political question, and I hope it will never be approached as such. I am at one with him in that, and I think all members of the committee are.
[Mr. Bradette.l
I do not think it was ever suggested when
this expedition went to Hudson bay that in one short season it could cover that whole immense area. Without for a moment calling in question the findings of that commission, and without calling in question the suggestion of my hon. friend that a further and more prolonged examination might result in finding deep sea fish in those waters, may I point out this, especially with reference to his suggestion that possibly the examination was not as complete as it might have been, and that if deep sea fish were discovered in those waters it would minimize the opportunity of selling fish from the Atlantic coast-

I say there were
rumours to that effect.

I never heard of them
before, but I do not find fault with my hon. friend for having voiced them, although I do not think there is any truth in them at all. I would point out that the fishing operations were under the direction of Captain Sigurd Sorensen, master of the Loubyrne. He was given full charge of the actual fishing operations, while the scientific aspect of the expedition were under the direct supervision of the officer in charge, Mr. H. B. Hachey. In Captain Sorensen the department had a man who had had twenty-four years of experience in trawler operations in various north Atlantic waters, including the North sea, the White sea, the gulf of St. Lawrence, the waters off Labrador, Iceland and the west coast of Scotland, and the region extending from the Grand banks to Georges banks. In addition, at least two members of the crew were experienced in the use of hand lines and long lines. The instructions received from the department were as follows-I am quoting from the report:
Actual fishing operations should be begun as soon after Hudson strait is entered as may be deemed feasible, but there should be no unnecessary loss of time to the trawler incurred in the journey to Churchill, or fishing carried on to the extent that might endanger exhaustion of the coal supply before Churchill would be reached. Also fishing should be conducted -again in the strait on the homeward journey to as great an extent as conditions will permit.
My hon. friend quoted quite correctly the number of hours which the expedition employed in the various methods of fishing. For example, that some seven hours and fifteen minutes were employed in the use of hand lines, twelve hours for drift nets, two hours and fifty-five minutes for long lines, and fifty-seven hours and fifty minutes fishing by means of the trawler, but when you come to analyze the record as disclosed in the report of the expedition it will be found that this com-

Supply-Fisheries
paratively limited number of hours represented continuous operations subject only to the limitations of weather and sea conditions, beginning on August 8 and continuing to September 10. Furthermore, these operations were directed by men who knew, of their own experience, from the character of the ground the probable places in which fish might be caught. So it by no means represented as limited an inquiry as my hon. friend would imagine. Furthermore, the scientific end of the expedition was engaged in determining a number of other factors which would have a bearing on evidencing whether or not there were any deep sea fish, such as taking the temperature at various depths, taking water samples, investigations as to the various forms of bottom life, quantitative and qualitative samples of minute organisms in the upper fifteen fathoms. If, as time proceeds, it is deemed advisable to extend and enlarge this experiment, I am prepared to approach it sympathetically. Certainly our store of knowledge will be much more rapidly augmented now that the Hudson bay railway is open and Churchill will become an occupied place of some importance. -Possibly we may be able to discover what the conditions are by the actual operations of men upon the ground, which would save the treasury a great deal of money in sending an expedition up there to carry on an investigation covering two or three years. If there is evidence that further and more complete and extended inquiries would result in the discovery of sea fish there I should be very happy to lend my support to the proposal,

Before this item is carried I should like again to bring before the house a matter which seriously concerns Canadian fishermen on the Pacific coast. At an earlier date I believe I outlined their reasons for being concerned about this particular matter. At this time, speaking again to the question, I shall quote some of the evidence by members of the American fishing fleet from Washington. The whole report is lengthy, and I do not intend at this time to read it fully, but shall make a few quotations to show that it is necessary for the American fishing fleet to use the port of Prince Rupert.
I understand that since I last spoke concerning this matter the minister has received a petition signed by fishermen and residents of Prince Rupert and vicinity. I understand it is signed by the Canadian Fishermen's Association. In 1920 it was urged that the port of Prince Rupert should be closed to American fishermen. I believe the minister has thoroughly investigated the matter, and that 22110-260

a wire from the Deep Sea Fishermen's Union. The wire is dated June 22, 1931, from Seattle, and is addressed to Mr. J. M. Morrison, the Canadian agent of the Deep Sea Fishermen's Union. The text is as follows:
Rumours here that there is strong move to close Prince Rupert to American vessels, wire our member's attitude on this matter. In my opinion it would not help men there as we are in the midst of a national and international depression we can and will try to have the tariff on Canadian fresh halibut reduced to one cent per pound if the men there think that of sufficient benefit.
I wish to read at this time a paragraph from a letter from myself to the minister dated July 2, 1931:
I also have a letter informing me that the halibut fishermen on the American side have asked their representative in Washington to cooperate in every way with the Canadian authorities in order to adjust the present discrimination between Canadian and American halibut fishermen, especially in reducing the American duty, if not altogether, at least 50 per cent. This is for your information and I hope you will give it due consideration and advise me as to what steps you have taken in this regard.
I do not think it is necessary to go into this matter at greater length. I wish merely to learn from the minister whether he has done anything to assist the fishermen either by negotiations with Washington or closing the port of Prince Rupert to American fishermen.

Before the minister answers
may I add my support to the proposals put forth by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Hanson), as I did when the same constituency was represented by an hon. member of the party opposite. This is not a political matter at all; it is beyond and I hope above that. The petition to which my hon. friend has referred I understand was signed by 1,500 people. I suppose that they did not solicit the ladies, so that 1,500 people in a place the size of Prince Rupert would indicate almost complete unanimity. I believe they seek to have the minister take steps to restrict the operation of American fishermen into the port of Prince Rupert. On many occasions in the past this matter has been discussed by officials but never was there a better opportunity or more appropriate occasion to take action than the present.
We know of the conditions of hardship existing among the fishermen in the present year, and I believe conditions will be much worse this year than they were last. Any support which can be given the fishermen to enable them to help themselves is much better than the handing out of doles. A gov-

ernment is in power committed to the policy of high protection. To avoid possibility of an argument I shall simply use the expression "protection." Coupled with that policy we have heard the further suggestion of equal opportunities to the man in Canada as against competitors from foreign fields. It cannot be said that Canadians and aliens are operating on equal terms when the alien can come into our ports, bond his fish through to the United States, get two cents a pound of protection in that market-because there is a duty on our fish going into the United States-fish with our fishermen on a common fishing ground and purchase gasoline at a price much lower than that asked of our fishermen.
At no time have we any right to object to duties imposed by foreign nations. That is their privilege. When such duties are imposed we can but take such steps as are possible to balance the situation. That is not always possible, but in this particular situation it is, owing to the geographical advantage we possess. The halibut ground used to be much nearer Seattle but because that ground has been fished out the fishermen have moved farther north and west until now it is practically compulsory for American fishermen to land their fish at Prince Rupert. There exists in the United States a rather high-class market such as we do not have in Canada. So we must base all our conclusions on those premises, that the market is in the United States. The halibut banks now being exploited lie so much nearer Prince Rupert that, as I said, the American fisherman is compelled to go in there, even though he does not want to. Efforts have been made to go to Ketchikan, which is comparatively near, or to Seattle, but in both cases it has been found impracticable and unprofitable, on account of the extra handling and extra expense involved. So the American fisherman must use the port of Prince Rupert, and the report that my friend from Skeena quoted was the report of a representative of the American fishing interests before a congressional committee at Washington, saying they did not want to change the existing system, and if they were compelled to they would have to tie up their boats.
The minister cannot impose a duty, but it is suggested that to remedy the present unsatisfactory situation he could charge port dues on all foreign fish coming into Prince Rupert. Or for a time he could withdraw the regulations under P.C. 2777, which gives certain privileges to American citizens coming into our ports. These privileges are granted absolutely as a matter of courtesy, and are

renewed annually at the beginning of the year. I do not suggest that he should do that; he need not close the port, but he could place our men on the same basis as the American fishermen by imposing port dues of 2 cents a pound on foreign fish. The evidence quoted by my hon. friend from Skeena shows that the American fishermen could not endure that. That is the language they used a year or two ago. But to show that condition still exists and is indeed intensified, we have only to consider that when this matter was brought up in the house a month or two ago-and it was not at the time pushed to the extreme of asking for action

immediately the American fishermen from their headquarters at Seattle wired, as my hon. friend has said, to Prince Rupert, asking the Canadian fishermen to go slow on that matter because they were making efforts with their congressmen at Washington to have the two cent duty taken off. We have evidence that they are taking the matter up now, and they are asking their congressmen to take action-and this only on a vague hint that the policy I have suggested might be adopted. I am thoroughly satisfied that if the minister took that step we would find that the American authorities, through pressure at Washington would arrange the matter by striking out the obnoxious two cent duty. The result would be as Mr. Lokken said, the duty would either have to be taken off or they would lose the trade. Either event would undoubtedly inure to the benefit of our fishermen and would be the making of Prince Rupert.
While it would benefit Prince Rupert both as to halibut and salmon as the duty on fish going into the United States applies not only to the halibut but to salmon, and that affects also the district which I represent. There is a season of the year when practically our only market for spring salmon is in the United States. Speaking a few minutes ago when I said that our market for halibut was almost exclusively in the eastern United States I should have also mentioned spring salmon. Our market for the spring salmon that we catch off the west coast of Vancouver island in the spring and early summer i3 principally in New York and other eastern United States cities. That market cannot be secured anywhere else, so far as I am aware, than in the United States and our nearest port is Seattle. If this regulation were passed we would get a better price for our "springs" as they are called, at that season of the year.
I hope the minister will take action. I may say, without any attempt to flatter him, that he has shown himself to be a man capable
of taking decided action. If he took action in this case he would not only endear himself to the fishing industry of the Pacific coast, but I think he would also secure the respect of our friends to the south, because that is just the sort of language they understand, and if they found that he was prepared to take a step such as I have suggested, it would buttress him very strongly in any dealings with them. I am quite sure we would soon find them knocking at our door anxious to enter into negotiations.

Mr. Chairman, my hon. friends, the members for Skeena and for Comox-Alberni have touched upon a question which is not free from difficulty, but in that respect it is in common with every problem that I have so far met in the fishing industry -it seems to be one of a succession of difficult and almost insolvable questions. Let me say at the outset that, while I agree with my horn friend from Comox-Alberni that this is not a political question so far as parties in Canada are concerned, yet he was unfortunate in bringing in the controversial question of protection, because I am rather sensitive upon the subject. Although a protectionist, let me say to him that I have never subscribed to the point of view that there is any such thing as high protection or low protection. I would not wish to digress into a tariff discussion, but I should not like his remarks upon that point to pass without putting in this caveat; otherwise he might accept my silence as agreement with his idea of what our views are in respect to that vexed question also.
As my hon. friend from Skeena knows, this subject probably has become more acute this year by reason of the depressed conditions which have resulted in a very low price for fish and a very limited market. In fact the market this year was limited to such an extent that something has happened there which so far as I can ascertain has never happened heretofore, certainly not on the Pacific coast, namely, the fishermen could not sell their fish and for a time had to tie up their vessels with heavy loss to themselves because their overhead charges had to be carried on in the meantime. I can quite understand the feeling of bitter dissatisfaction-I do not think that is too strong a term to use -of those engaged in the industry at the unfairness of the situation which exists there today by reason of the difference in prices. Because here we find American vessels and Canadian vessels fishing side by side in the same waters, for the same fish, with the same
Supply-Fisheries

gear, and coming to the same port, and eaeh having the same privileges there, and yet the American fisherman can ship his fish through Canada into the United States and land it there duty free, while the Canadian fisherman is handicapped to the extent of the duty of two cents a pound. I must say that I do not take very much exception to the attitude of the Canadian halibut fisherman as to the injustice of that situation. I can assure my hon. friend that I have given very serious thought to the question as to whether it would not be wise for us to prohibit the port privileges at Prince Rupert to the American halibut fishing fleet so long as this unfair condition continues. That I did not take action was because the petitions to which my hon. friend refers came to hand within the last ten days, I think, certainly not more than two weeks ago.
This scheme has only crystallized, if I may use the word, within that period of time. It would be a very unfair thing, I think, to take such drastic action in the midst of a fishing season after a large fleet of vessels had left their ports, outfitted and undertaken their season's operation with the idea quite properly in mind when they started that the conditions which hitherto obtained would continue to obtain during the fishing season. But I may say to my hon. friend that the department is giving very serious consideration to the question of whether we would not be wise to close the port of Prince Rupert to the American fishing fleet under these conditions, so that to the extent to which it can be utilized it may be made available to our Canadian fishermen. I would regret to have to take that step, in view of the fact that there are a number of questions outstanding between ourselves and the United States with regard to fisheries matters. I would rather approach those questions around a common table in the hope of being able to reach a solution which would be reasonably satisfactory; in other words I would rather approach our American friends in an attitude of sweet reasonableness.

You would not be red
blooded, like the Minister of Railways?

Sometimes the red blooded policy is the policy required; sometimes the other is the policy required, and I will say to my hon. friend that I will have no hesitation in using whatever policy happens to be necessary, as far as I am concerned.
I want to impress upon my hon. friends and members of the committee generally, that I am fully seized of the seriousness of this
[Mr* Rhodes.]
problem. As I have said, I would wish that it might be solved by our sitting around a council table and discussing the matter with our American friends in an endeavour to reach a solution which might be reasonably satisfactory.

I understand
negotiations are already under way between the United States government and the Canadian government with regard to this question of duty.

I would not wish to say
very much about that at this stage, but I can assure my hon. friend that the department has not lost a single moment in taking every step and using every reasonable effort in an endeavour to lead the way to a solution. The department will continue to keep this matter in mind; it will not be lost sight of and no effort will be spared to see if we cannot reach a solution which will be reasonably satisfactory all around.

Hon. members will excuse us from British Columbia for taking up the time of the committee in these matters, but the fishing industry is as important to us as wheat growing is important to the prairies, and whether hon. members like it or not they will have to allow us a reasonable time in which to discuss these questions.
I think the hon. member for Skeena and myself might well join in thanking the minister for the attitude he has taken. Knowing him to be a man of his word I believe he will do even moi'e than he has indicated I should like to deal with one or two other matters, but before doing so I should like to express my gratitude to the minister, if I may do so without the suggestion of trying to curry favour with him, for his action in connection with the pilchard industry this spring. To his energy and persistence alone was due the fact that the regulations were so changed that it is now possible to manufacture pilchard oil into shortening in Canada and, thus cairry on a very important industry in British Columbia. Previously the regulations were such that it was impossible to do so; our main market was in the United States, with a very high duty and a very low price, and many of the plants were bankrupt while others were almost prepared to shut down. The minister had the regulations changed so that now we will have access to the Canadian market. The effect of this action may not be apparent this year, because probably it will be necessary for a plant to be built in order to carry out the process of hydrogenation, which is the essential part of the manufacture, but even the knowledge that this

Supply-Fisheries
market is available has enabled several additional plants to be put into operation. I see by the press that there is a very good run of pilchard, and it'is to be hoped this change will make more money available for an industry which I can assure the house very badly needs it.
Some six weeks or two months ago the canned salmon industry in British Columbia was very much agitated by a report, which there seems to be good reason to believe to be true, that the French parliament was preparing to introduce a bill which would have the effect of doubling the general tariff on canned salmon, thus giving the Japanese, who are under a different trade treaty, complete control of that market. At one time we sold a large proportion of a certain variety of our fish in France, and if nothing can be done to modify or change this provision the result will be disastrous. I should like to ask the minister if anything has been done or if it will be possible to do anything in that regard.

The last question asked by the hon. member for Comox-AIberni is one of exreme delicacy. Of course he is aware that the disparity in favour of the Japanese has existed ever since the French treaty came into operation.
Yes, but this makes it worse.

Unfortunately that disparity has been such that it has brought about a gradual decrease in our shipments of canned salmon to France and has deflected to Japan what hitherto had been an almost exclusively Canadian business. That situation is still further aggravated by recent tariff changes made by the French government, which will make it practically impossible for us to export our canned salmon to that country. All I can say to my hon. friend is this: The hon. gentleman will realize that it is purely within the right of the French government to effect such tariff changes as may suit their own purposes, but to the extent that it is open to us to discuss the -matter with the government of France I can assure my hon. friend that this will be done. So far as any action of ours will enable us to bring about a betterment of that condition, it will be the desire of the government to endeavour to have this country placed on a parity of trade with our friendly neighbour, Japan.
How much longer must we put up with this French treaty?
My hon. friend will have to address that question to the Prime Minister.

One more point before I go home; after this I will not bother anyone further. My last point is in connection with facilitating methods of communication to a place called Kyuquot on the west coast of Vancouver island. On this occasion I can hardly resist making my annual protest in connection with the diversion of $160,000- I see the hon. member for Ddgby-Anmapolis is not here-to the friends of the hon. member on the Atlantic while we on the Pacific are equally entitled to it. I am not going to say anything more on that point now, except to suggest that since they have been getting the whole of that sum illegally for a long period of years-it is a fisheries bounty authorized by statute, and I am not going into it in detail-we on the Pacific should be entitled to the major portion of the vote now under consideration, this $190,000 for the conseivation and development of deep sea fisheries and the furthering of the demand for fish. I assure the minister that we will not ask that it be expended in the petty ways in which the money is spent on the Atlantic, where they give eight dollars and six bits to one man and seventy-five cents to some other. That is not going to develop deep sea fisheries.
At the annual meeting of the Pacific coast fisheimen, held at Nanaimo last December, when the Deputy Minister of Fisheries was present, a petition was either presented or referred to from those who fish from the Kyuquot asking for better wire facilities. Kyuquot is a very small place; I do not suppose the total population exceeds 50 people during the winter, but when the fishing season is on the population may run up to 2,000, because many fishermen use that village as a base. I may explain also that Kyuquot is very remote; the nearest telegraph wire is about seventy miles away, and the country between is of such a character that one might almost say it would be impossible to build a telegraph line there. Nothing is impossible if you have sufficient money, but this countiy is so cut up with inlets, fiords and so forth, and the ground itself is so rough that the expenditure would be prohibitive. These people fish during the spring and summer, and in these days of keen competition it is necessary to have access to market information. A telegraph line eighty miles away is of very little use, they must have constant contact with the outside world. A sudden run of fish might come along and they would have them on the ground and not be able to get a carrier in time. These are the conditions which they have to face. A gentleman writes

The first reaction to the
information that this business amounts to $200,000 per year is that it should be sufficiently profitable to enable those engaged in it to provide their own means of communication.

These are small fishermen
with no money.

This subject has been up
before and is being inquired into at the present time. I do not think that this department should embark upon a policy of establishing telegraph and wireless services. We have neither the machinery nor the equipment, and I do not think it is good business to have several departments conducting similar lines of endeavour. The Department of Marine handles all wireless matters, and I understand telegraph lines are being operated by both that department and the Department of Public Works. I assure my hon. friend that I will take this matter up with the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), and if it can be demonstrated that this is a reasonable measure of assistance which this department can give at not too great an expense, I will be disposed to consider the matter favourably.

Mr. Chairman, speaking
for the other end of the Dominion, I want to say a word or two in support of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). I am glad that the minister appears to be somewhat sympathetic in this regard. Every

means possible should be used to extend our market for fish in the United States. This matter affects the western fisheries, but I think the minister knows better than most of us that it affects even more the eastern fisheries. I appreciate that the minister cannot give any definite information with regard to the progress of international negotiations, nor do I desire to instruct or advise him in this connection, but it seems to me that if we were able to go to Washington with this Prince Rupert matter and indicate to our friends to the south that we have been doing them a favour in affording certain facilities, there would be a different situation existing as far as the exporting of fish is concerned. I feel sure my hon. friend has now found that the negotiations, which were held up only because of certain negotiations with regard to treaties which were being considered, have sufficiently progressed to enable him to reopen the matter-and I presume he has done so-and to endeavour to secure better terms and more opportunities in connection with the consumption of fish in the United States. I assure him that so far as I am concerned he will have all support in that respect, and I am glad to hear he is at least thinking of this matter of withdrawing the port privilege or thinking of the extent to which it affords facilities to United States fishermen and of the way in which it might be said to improve our relations with the United States. The fishermen of Nova Scotia, as the minister knows, needs that market very badly. While we welcome every effort that can be made to extend the Canadian market, I am not convinced that the Canadian market can absorb the production of fish which it is possible to have if a decent and fair market is provided for the fishermen.
The minister spoke of the fishing industry in the west, and I have no doubt he intended to include the fishing industry in the east also. I do not think in any previous year the fishermen of the east have endured a worse situation or more hardships, if I may use that term in connection with business, than they did this year. Prices have been down; gear has been lost; it has been difficult to make ends meet; there has been no market and altogether the fishing industry is not at this time in a very healthy condition. It would give the fishermen new hope if the minister could indicate that there was some prospect of the opening up of the United States market.
While I am on my feet, I should like to ask what progress has been made with regard to the survey which I understand is being made by the firm of Cockfield Brown and
Company with regard to the development of increased marketing facilities for fish.

I wish to thank the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth for the subject matter of his remarks and his manner of approaching it. With every word he has said I am in hearty accord. The fishermen in the eastern part of Canada have had a very serious year and every reasonable effort ought to be made to assist them.
My hon. friend knows how delicate his first question is as to negotiations with the United States. I can speak only in general terms and assure him that I am at one with him in appreciation of the desirability of what he has suggested. I feel sure when the time comes I shall be able to demonstrate to him that we have not lost any opportunity to take every step we can towards that end.
The survey of Cockfield, Brown and Company is now completed; the report is in process of preparation, and last week I was advised by Doctor Goforth that according to an agreement it will be in my hands on the first day of August. That survey, contrary to a more or less general impression, is not by any means confined to the Canadian market. It covers marketing conditions throughout the world wherever there is a possibility for a market. I am led to believe it has been very comprehensive and I trust when the report is available we shall be able to base upon it a policy which will enable us to enlarge not only our Canadian market but our foreign market to a considerable extent.
Does my hon. friend think the report will be available at the end of August or within a month?
As soon as it is in hand and has been perused, we shall have it printed and made available for distribution if possible before the end of August, or at all events as early as may be.

I know the report is not confidential except in the sense that it should be given to the government first. From what my hon. friend knows of what has been discussed and the nature of the report, does he think that under the present legislation and powers of the department any recommendations contained in the report can be put into effect?

I do not think any further legislation will be required, nor do I think, so far as this year is concerned, any further appropriations will be necessary for the purposes which we have in mind.

Has any request been received from the salmon fishermen for an extension, of time? If so, what action has been taken?

I think I could answer the question of the hon. member for Gloucester without making any inquiry at all. I do not know there has ever been a year or a district that there has not been a request for an extension of not only salmon fishing but every other kind. Perhaps my hon. friend will take that as an answer.
I should like to know what action he has taken.

I do not think this discussion of the fishing industry would be complete if I did not put in a word in regard to Quebec. In the early spring I received many complaints from those engaged in the salmon fisheries on account of the change in the regulations. Has the minister reason to believe the change made in working out in the interests of the fishermen and the fishing industry in that part of the country?

My hon. friend may take it as axiomatic that no regulations and no change in any regulations will ever be satisfactory to everyone. The best that the department can hope to do is to make regulations and effect such changes as will reduce complaints to the minimum. My information from the officers of my department is that the changes recently effected have been in the main reasonably satisfactory. They have been concurred in by the fishery authorities of the province of Quebec and by our officers, and I think on the whole are supported by public opinion, although here and there no doubt there will be the odd complaint.

I suppose under this item I may refer to the policy which the minister enunciated the other day in the house with regard to trawlers. I note he intimates he has come to the conclusion-and I take it he is enunciating a matter of government policy -'that any trawler to be licensed must be built and owned in Canada. Does the minister intend to pass regulations to that effect?

Yes. Regulations are now being prepared, and I propose to recommend them to my colleagues. If they concur, the regulations will be put into force. I presume my hon. friend gathers from what I have said previously that it would 'be unjust to discriminate against trawlers already licensed, but it does not follow that we shall continue to license them all. If it be found that four or five trawlers are sufficient, we shall not

license more than that number, but the six that are now in existence will have the preference.
My hon. friend is going to pass regulations?
Yes.
Let me steer my hon. friend past any pitfalls that the late government found. Is he not going to get into difficulty if he passes regulations of that kind?
I do not say that we arc going to avoid pitfalls, whatever we do, but if my hon. friend has any suggestions to make I shall be glad to receive them.

In order that it may be put beyond peradventure, in view of the fact that a case is pending before the supreme court, my hon. friend should1 have a statute for whatever he is going to do, particularly in the matter of limitation of licences. I am all for limitation of licences. As my hon. friend knows, the policy of the government of which I had the honour to be member was that after April 1, 1932, no licences should be granted except to Canadian-built trawlers. I understand that the difference between that policy and the policy enunciated by my hon. friend is that after this date no licences will be granted to other than Canadian-built trawlers except such as are now in existence and are now licensed.

I think my hon. friend,
if he will look at section 69 (A) will agree that it gives ample powers to the minister; in fact, as I said the other day, it gives too much power to the minister. I wish it had not given quite so much. I do not think any power, desirable or undesirable, could possibly be added by legislative authority to the powers contained in that section. This need have no bearing on the case now on appeal before the supreme court. That is only a question whether we are going to take so much money out of the trawler companies or not. If my colleagues agree with me in the regulations to be promulgated, I am going to recommend that that case be withdrawn and not proceeded with, because there is no object in attempting to extract large amounts of money from companies which are already having difficulties in financing. So I say quite frankly that the case was held over on my recommendation, having in mind the course which I felt I ought to take. If that course is taken, that case will be withdrawn.

I do not want my hon.
friend to misunderstand me. I do not recede

one tittle from the position which the former government took. We believe the policy which we laid down in that order in council was correct. The exchequer court has decided that it was ultra vires, but I am talking of the policy as a policy, and so far as I am concerned it still stands. On the other hand, I would warn my hon. friend, if I may, with deference, that in view of the principle which seems to have been laid down by Mr. Justice Audette, it would seem to me that he ought to look very carefully into the question whether he can ever make a regulation limiting the licences to the trawlers now in existence, for that, I understand, is what he is going to do. Outside of that they are to be Canadian-built trawlers. That is one of the points on which Mr. Justice Audette decided that the order in council was ultra vires. I only throw out that suggestion to my hon. friend. I think he is not going far enough in his limitations, but if he is going that far, I do not want him coming to us next year and saying: Well, we passed regulations, and we found that they were ultra vires. In view of the principle laid down by Mr. Justice Audette it is very questionable whether the policy which my hon. friend laid down in the house the other day can be accomplished without legislation.

I do not propose to enter into a discussion of the legai phases. I can assure my hon. friend that the question he has raised I have had in mind, and I certainly do not anticipate any difficulty upon that score. If the regulations are not so onerous as to come within the purview of the judgment of Mr. Justice Audette, and I do not think they will be, I cannot see where we shall have any difficulty.

Item agreed to.
Oyster culture, $10,000.

I would like to direct the
attention of the committee and of the minister in particular to a state of affairs that exists in connection with oysters in British Columbia. We have two rivers there, the Serpentine and the Nicomekl, flowing into what is known as Mud bay. These two rivers have been set aside for biological purposes presumably for the cultivation of oysters. In order to acquaint the minister with the situation as it now exists I should like to give him a few facts of the case.
At one time there were no dams in these two rivers, but a few years ago dams were constructed across them and about the same time a lease was given by the provincial government to companies to propagate
oysters out in the bay. It was not until the dams had been constructed, and possibly not until the oyster operations began in the bay that the oysters began to go up these rivers. The dams are each about three and a half miles from the bay. There were however native oysters in the riveTs before these companies started their operations in the bay. The beds of the rivers are now covered with old shells to a depth of some four or five feet, and the fishermen last year had a great-deal of difficulty in fishing in these rivers because their nets would catch on these oyster beds, and when they dragged up their nets they would bring up large masses of oyster shells and also oysters which tore holes in the nets. Many persons were coming to these rivers to take oysters, but the oyster companies frowned on such action. They claimed that the oysters on the rivers belonged to them, due to their having propagated the oysters for many years and having also brought spat from away back east. They then approached the provincial government, which in turn approached the federal government. The result was that these oyster beds were set aside for biological purposes.
May I point out to the minister that in the description as it appears in the return that was brought down, an error occurs, inasmuch as it states that the reserve would exist from the river to Boundary bay. I think that that should be checked up because Boundary bay is far off, and if the reserve really extended to those limits not even the company could take oysters, because Boundary bay is many miles distant from Mud bay, into which these two rivers flow. I have the official file before me, from which I should like to quote. Here is a letter addressed to Mr. Found by J. P. Babcock, assistant to the commissioner of the provincial Fisheries department, Victoria. He says:
It is suggested that you take the bull by the horns and create an oyster reserve.
That certainly is an Irishism, to take the bull by the horns and create an oyster reserve. In another letter from Mr. C. R. Elsey, the marine biologist in charge of the oyster investigation, to Mr. J. P. Babcock, this statement appears:
Shells placed in the rivers by the Crescent Company have become heavily set.
I may say, Mr. Chairman, that no shells were set in the river by the company. The shells were there in the bay already, so that statement is not correct. He says further:
Efforts on the part of the oyster company to obtain leases have failed.
That is probably correct, Mr. Chairman, because there is a controversy as to the
