respective jurisdiction of the Dominion and provincial government over navigable streams, the Dominion government having jurisdiction over navigable rights and the provincial government claiming the bed of the stream. He says further:
Persons have been taking these oysters but the Crescent Oyster Company has refrained in the past from such action, but are at present quite resentful of such unrestricted vandalism and threaten, quite naturally, to go in with their superior equipment.
It would be interesting to know what superior equipment can be used in lifting oysters, because my information is that oysters are lifted "by hand. He says further:
The removal of these fully grown and well established oysters would make the summer's work futile and put back for ten years the establishing of seed beds.
That is very far away from the truth, because those beds have so many oysters in them now that they could not be depleted in years. One firm has offered $100,000 for the privilege of getting the oysters from each of the rivers, so great are the numbers of oysters in them. So that the statement that the removal of these fully grown and well established oysters would make the summer's work futile and put back for ten years the establishing of seed beds, is not correct.
One of the criticisms I have to offer concerns the hardship enforced upon fishermen. Fishing licences are given every year to fishermen allowing operations on certain areas on those rivers. Until last year they had the right to take the oysters and sell them if they wished, or use them for their own purposes. Now that privilege has been denied them. On behalf of those fishermen I ask the minister seriously to consider this point of view:	They are now denied the
right of taking oysters from those rivers. It is hardly correct to say that the beds of those streams have been set aside for experimental purposes. No experiment is necessary, because the oysters are there by the thousands. In fact, when they lifted the gates off the dams this year, oysters were found encrusted about two feet thick upon them. The fact of the matter is that the company to which I have referred are endeavouring to obtain absolute control of the two rivers. They could not obtain control in any other -way than by first coming here and having the reserve put on for biological purposes. This is the first move. - Their intention later on is to obtain possession, but in the meantime outsiders including fishermen who year after year have used these streams for fishing are denied the right even to use

the oysters for themselves. I have not gone into full particulars with the minister, but I should like to have done so because there are many aspects of the matter which should be inquired into. First of all I am asking on behalf of the fishermen that they receive back the right to get the oysters. Secondly, I think the situation should be carefully looked into; in the event of any lease being given to a company to operate the question of navigable rights would come in, because the rivers might have to be dredged. If any company or companies owned the beds of the rivers they would object very strenuously to dredging operations as such operations would take out practically all the oysters from the river. I shall not take up further the time of the committee, but would ask that the minister give these matters his serious consideration.

The only manner in which I can be of service to my hon. friend is to send his remarks as they wifi be reported in Hansard to the Commissioner of Fisheries of British Columbia, because the fisheries to which he has referred come within the exclusive jurisdiction of that province. It is true that we must in all cases, and did in this case, pass regulations, but that was done at the request of the government of British Columbia, pursuant to the policy followed by this as well as by previous administrations, namely to put into effect only such regulations as are in conformity with the wishes of the various provincial governments. That arrangement is subject always to a general provision-in the event of the dominion not agreeing with the provinces on a matter of policy relating to conservation, or something of that nature. So it was that this regulation was passed at the request of the government of British Columbia, and the area was set aside to enable experiments to be conducted by the biological board. Those experiments were paid for by the Dominion but were carried out by the biological board for the province of British Columbia and at its request. At the moment I do not believe I can do more than send Hansard containing the remarks of my hon. friend to the Commissioner of Fisheries for the province of British Columbia.
What experiments were carried on last year?-because I can assure you no experiments are necessary. Oysters are there on each river for a distance of three and a half miles-beds of them.

I think my hon. friend will find that a report covering these experiments

Supply-Fisheries
has been circulated by the biological board. In any event I believe there is a report in the department which will be made available to him.

I have in mind a matter which may not be of very great importance, but for the consideration of which I would ask special permission at this time. It concerns an appointment, and is as important to those interested as would be a matter of international significance to the industry at large. I am protesting on behalf of my own constituency. Mr. Marshall was appointed inspector in Digby. He had been dismissed for active political partisanship about a year before. However, in the eyes of the government at least he had purged his sin and was again considered eligible. Mr Lewis had been appointed temporarily and was located at Yarmouth. An advertisement was issued by the Civil Service Commission, confined to the counties of Halifax, Guysborough, and Digby. There was a joint advertisement for Kings and Queens but Yarmouth was not included. The point I make is that Yarmouth is included in that particular fishing district. The inspector who was to be appointed was to have jurisdiction in Yarmouth, Digby, Lunenburg and Queens, but when the advertisement was issued Yarmouth was excluded; in other words no residents of Yarmouth need apply. Why was that?

I cannot agree entirely with my hon. friend. I remember the matter to which he refers. Digby is a more central region for this officer than is the town of Yarmouth. Yarmouth is at one end of the area, because that inspector covers the counties of Yarmouth, Shelburne, Queens Digby Lunenburg and Annapolis. His location at Yarmouth would put him about as far away as possible from the centre of the area.
It would put him just in the centre.

No, I do not agree with my hon. friend. Digby is a much more central point. He has to go away up to cover Annapolis, Queens and Lunenburg. Certainly when in Digby he is much nearer the centre thaD if he were in Yarmouth. My hon. friend will recall that we insisted the offices should remain at Digby where they had been originally.

My hon. friend has missed the point. I am not talking about the location of the offices. I say my hon. friend is wrong; anybody who would take the trouble to look at the map would know that he is wrong.
With his knowledge of the geography of the province of Nova Scotia he does not need to look at the map. Yarmouth is in the centre of that district. Fishery inspectors have to go around the shores. For the first time, Yarmouth was going to have the office, but my hon. friend moved it back to Digby.
It never was moved to Yarmouth.
Let us leave it at that; but when my hon. friend moves it to Digby why does he exclude all the residents of Yarmouth from eligibility for the position?
We are not discussing the matter to which the hon. member for Shelburne-Yar-mout'h (Mr. Ralston) has directed attention.
I asked special permission to have the matter considered.

I have no objection to discussing it. I do not agree with my hon. friend at all when he says the jurisdiction of the fishery officers is around the shores; it is over the rivers and streams and lakes as well. So he covers the Whole area. My hon. friend was wrong there.

One-tenth of the rivers,
streams and shore.

Yarmouth was not excluded. This question would never have arisen, because Mr. Lewis was not dismissed. He was asked to carry on his office from Digby, where quarters were available in the public building, and where the work had been carried on for years and years. If Mr. Lewis had not resigned he would have been in office yet, and it was only when we insisted on his living in Digby that he resigned. Having resigned, his place was filled by the Civil Service Commission.

I understand that, but
it has nothing to do with my question. I am asking why when the position was going to be filled in Digby residents of Yarmouth were not allowed to apply.
My hon. friend had better address his question to the Civil Service Commission.

My hon. friend knows
perfectly well that the advertisements were prepared by the department.

Quite so, but the position
was filled by the Civil Service Commission.
Supply-Fisheries

A gentleman, a returned
soldier, living in Yarmouth was declared ineligible for the position because he lived outside the district advertised.

My deputy tells me that
it cannot be the same position; but even so. he has to live in Digby, that is all.

I am saying that according to this return this gentleman is regarded as ineligible for this position because he lived outside the district advertised. There was no advertisement that included Yarmouth. Halifax and Digby were included.

Will my hon. friend let
me have the advertisement?
Yes.

My hon. friend is confusing two things. This advertisement is for an inspector of fisheries; that would be a Digby county appointment. Mr. Marshall's position was that of supervisor of fisheries-a different office altogether.
Was not Clement Crowell an applicant for this position?

He may have been, but
this advertisement has nothing to do with the appointment to the position at Digby.

Is the other position
filled by a returned soldier?

My deputy advises me
that we have two vacancies for an inspector of fisheries in Digby county; that is why they were asked to be residents of Digby. The position that my hon. friend speaks of is that of supervisor. Of course, there is no question of exclusion there, and it was quite competent for the man at Yarmouth to apply. I do not know anything as to the details.

I simply want to say to
my hon. friend that that is the information given me by the secretary who abstracted the return.
Quite so. But possibly the individual referred to in this application might also have applied for the position of supervisor.

Yes. Is it true or not
that for the position of supervisor residents of the county of Yarmouth were excluded?
No.
Does my hon. friend know that?
I am so advised by my deputy.
Does my hon. friend know that Mr. Merkel was an applicant for the position of supervisor?
I would have to make inquiries to find out.
If my hon. friend would inquire I should be obliged. I do not want to do any injustice to my hon. friend or to the department.
I shall be glad to make inquiries.

A man named J. W. Merkel lived in Digby and served in France for four years. According to the report I have he was third on the list of eligibles. Even so, under the Civil Service Act he would be entitled primarily to the appointment, because no matter how far down the list a returned soldier happens to be he takes precedence over a civilian. Perhaps my hon. friend will at the same time look up the application of Clement W. Crowell. He was a disability case. He had a super-preference according to the return and applied for the position.
Yes, I will make inquiries.

Item agreed to.
To provide, subject to the approval of the governor in council, for a grant to the United Maritime Fishermen, $5,000.

Will my hon. friend be good enough to call the attention of his colleague, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ryckman) to a communication to the secretary of the United Maritime Fishermen? There was some difficulty in Yarmouth to which I have referred before in this house-I do not propose to go into it fully again on this occasion-with regard to holding up a shipment of rope on which cents dumping duty had been imposed temporarily. An investigation was held which took a considerable time. The net result was that the rope was finally released in time for the fishing season, but very late, and after the fishermen had been put to a great deal of trouble due to the uncertainty as to whether they would get the rope or not. Then the secretary of the United Maritime Fishermen-which is the association getting this vote-wrote to the minister of Customs with regard to the holding up of the shipment at Yarmouth and to be advised fully as to the conditions under which it was released. The reply sent from the Department of National Revenue-I am bringing it to the attention of the minister,

Supply-Fisheries
and I am sure he will see that such a thing does not occur again-is signed by Mr. Watson. He says:
Messrs. Stone and Forsyth, Boston, Mass., have been advised as to the conditions under which the importation at Yarmouth-referred to by you-was released and are in a position to communicate same to you if they so desire.
It does not make any difference who the secretary of the United Maritime Fishermen happens to be, he represents a responsible body recognized by this government in the vote now under consideration, and I submit that the information he asked for was information to which he was entitled, and that he should not have been referred to somebody in Boston when the required information was so easily available in the department.

I went very carefully into that case. My hon. friend, I think, is wrong in saying that this extra duty was charged. As a matter of fact, Mr. Breadner, acting for the department, wired to the collector in Yarmouth not to collect, but to assure himself that the shipment had come direct from Holland. That was where the whole question arose. It was thought at first that the rope had been transhipped at Boston, but when it was found that it had come direct from Holland it was passed through without extra duty. The inquiry had taken place before Doctor Hamer ever sent any telegram. I have in my hand a copy of the letter on the subject written by Stone & Forsyth and addressed to the Prime Minister.
I have it here.

May I say it is almost a disease with Doctor Hamer, the secretary of the United Maritime Fishermen, to rush into print on the first available opportunity, usually with a telegram, which he in all cases sends collect. In the present instance he could not resist dashing into print and getting his name-and usually his photograph-into the papers at the same time. Messrs. Stone & Forsyth say:
We feel that Dr. Hamer should have waited the result of the investigation and the decision to be made by Mr. Breadner's office before giving the matter such publicity.
In other words, the very people for whom he professed to speak in part, took exception to his having dashed into the newspapers before he knew what he was talking about. As a matter of fact this whole thing was adjusted by officials of the department, and Doctor Hamer had nothing whatever to do with it one way or the other. But he had to stick his telegram in the paper, get his photograph published once more and try to take a little credit in the matter.

I do not know and
never even saw Doctor Hamer, but I want to say to my hon. friend that he is not quite doing justice to the association.
Neither is Doctor Hamer.

My hon. friend said
Doctor Hamer had nothing to do with it. Here is a telegram from Mr. Breadner dated January 30 in which Mr. Breadner does not say "Hold it up" or "Do something temporarily," although he does say something about an investigation pending. The telegram reads:
Value for entry with collection of dumping duty twenty-three and one-half cents per pound less two and one-half cents per pound discount to dealers pending completion of investigation.
On February 1, only two days later, Doctor Hamer does wire, and I suppose there are wires from him right along. Then my hon. friend read a letter from Stone & Forsyth, for whom he said Doctor Hamer was acting. Stone & Forsyth are the dealers; they are not the fishermen. I am talking about the fishermen, and I only rose to make one point, that the secretary of the fishermen's association of the maritime provinces is entitled to some different answer than to be told that he can go to Boston and find out what was done there. That was the only point I desired to make, and I repeat it.

Item agreed to.
To provide for an investigation by an international committee into the probable effect upon the fisheries of the lower bay of Fundy region of damming Passamaquoddy and Cobseook hays, in New Brunswick and Maine, U.S.A., $22,500.

There are a few minutes
left before six o'clock, and I think we can get through this item, since I have just one question. Can the minister tell me what progress has been made with this investigation? I understand that the Canadian representatives to the commission already have been named in the persons of the Deputy Minister of Fisheries and Doctor Huntsman. If that is true I wish to express my satisfaction with those commissioners, but I should like to know how far the matter has progressed, because the delay is causing a great deal of uneasiness in the fishing industry of Passamaquoddy bay.

It is true that the Canadian representatives are the Deputy Minister of Fisheries and Doctor Huntsman, and I may say that the Deputy Minister of Fisheries has been appointed chairman of the joint board. There has been no delay so far as their efforts or the efforts of the department

Supply-Agriculture
have been concerned. As a matter of fact it has been difficult to get the best class of men to conduct the technical phases of the investigation, but there is on the way now one of the foremost experts of the British isles in matters touching the herring industry who, through the good offices of the British government, has been made available to this commission for a period of two years.

Item agreed to.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE INCREASED PENALTIES FOR VIOLATION

speechtext:
Mr. SAMUEL GOBEIL (Compton) moved the third reading of Bill No. 16, to amend the Dairy Industry Act.
Motion agreed to, and bill read the third time and passed.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE INCREASED PENALTIES FOR VIOLATION
speechtext: The orders under private and public bills having been exhausted the house will revert to committee of supply.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Fraser (Cariboo) in the chair.
Dairying, including grant of $5,000 to National Dairy Council, $295,000.

Mr. Chairman, would the minister advise the house why the price of milk for home consumption remains the same when the price of butter has dropped so considerably? The price of butter has dropped from 40 cents per pound last year to 20 cents

per pound this year, while the price of mils has remained at the same level for the past five years.
The only reason that can be given is that we are on an export basis with regard to butter and not with regard to whole milk
I understand an amendment was moved to this item when it was before the committee previously.

Yes. It was moved by Mr. Young, seconded by Mr. Bouchard:
That the item be reduced by $5,000, being the amount of a grant to the National Dairy council.
Amendment negatived on division.

I entirely agree with what the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) has said. Let me draw the attention of the committee to one recommendation in particular. But first let me take this opportunity of fulfilling a very pleasant duty in congratulating the hon. member who is acting as chairman of the committee (Mr. Fraser, Cariboo) upon attaining such a high position to-night. The recommendation I wish to
mention is that which the National Dairy Council makes with regard to a high tariff on butter. Last year the tariff on butter was six cents a pound, and during the September special session the government increased it to eight cents. I asked the question: When was the highest tariff imposed on butter? It was before the new Australian treaty was brought before the house; in other words, in April we had the highest tariff on butter since the discovery of Canada, and yet the price was the lowest since May, 1904. Therefore a high tariff was of no use in protecting the farmers because the tariff was the highest and yet the price was the lowest. Although the Prime Minister made some jokes about the numerous returns for which I asked, thanks to that return the government has changed its policy and is no more acting in accordance with the recommendations of the dairy council, but in the light of that return it has reduced the tariff to five cents a pound. The tariff on butter is now one cent a pound less than it was when the former government was in office. Perhaps this tariff will cure the evil in time, but I do not know how the^ platform and stump speakers we heard during the last campaign preaching high tariff in my constituency as in others throughout Quebec, will explain the good results of that high tariff policy. I cannot conceive that it was ever good for the farmer, and we have the evidence now. It shows that with time the government can improve a lot.

I am opposed to this item of $5,000 for the National Dairy Council on the ground that last year the activity of the National Dairy Council was simply pro-panganda for higher tariffs. All the creameries in Ontario and the National Dairy Council, of which they may or may not be members-
I am not clear on that point-spent all their energies in trying to convince the farmers .that protection on butter was going to give them a greater return. If the National Dairy Council would	set	itself	to	answering	thequestion asked	by	the	hon.	member	forTemiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) we might well grant them $5,000. The Minister of Agriculture did not answer that question; at least, he did not answer it wholly. While it is true that milk is sold at	home	and	butter is	soldabroad, I think,	it is also	true	that the	lack
of organization among the producers of milk and the organization of the distributors of milk have very much to do with the great spread between the price the producer receives and the price the consumer pays. I do feel that the consumers to-day are being almost, if not quite, as badly treated as the producers
Beauharnois Power-Report

of milk, because they are paying much more than they should pay under the circumstances, and the producers are getting much less than they should get. I am entirely opposed to this vote. As a matter of fact, I would say that outside of the Conservative party itself there was no more effective body of propagandists for protection in the last election than the National Dairy Council of Canada.

I see by Le Droit, in an
advertisement in its issue of July 24, that five-pound lots of butter are being sold at
15	cents per pound. I am entirely opposed to this grant of $5,000 to the National Dairy Council, and I would ask the minister to explain how it is that butter is being sold in five-pound lots in the city of Hull at 15 cents per pound.
It must be peanut butter.
No, it is good butter.

The hon. member for
Willow Bunch a few moments ago stated that the dairies in Ottawa were paying the farmers
16	and 17 cents per gallon of milk, but the dairies hare recently adopted a new rule that milk shipped to Ottawa and testing less than 3.25 would be paid for at the rate of 64 cents per 100 pounds, which is 6.02 cents per gallon. I do not want to refer to the question of paying a bounty to the wheat farmers of the west, but I do say that it is utterly impossible for the farmers to produce a gallon of milk for 6.02 cents. That milk is sold at very much higher prices to the consumer. I noted in the committee of agriculture this morning the very good disposition of the minister to inquire into the spread between the price to the producer and the price to the consumer. I would ask him to make a full inquiry into the milk business; to start by going into the capitalization of these dairy companies, and secondly to ascertain what they do with the milk that they buy from the farmers, and what revenue they derive from it. The middleman is getting far more profit than the farmer. There is ground there, and very serious ground, for a thorough investigation, in order that the producers may be assured that they are going to get some value for the products they deliver to the dairies.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.

speechtext: I desire to table the fourth report of the special committee appointed to investigate the Beauharnois project, and to give notice that on Thursday next I shall move that the report be concurred in. I give notice in order that in the meantime hon. members may acquaint themselves with its contents.

subtopic: FOURTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TABLED
speechtext: May I ask my right hon. friend if the report will appear in the Votes and Proceedings of to-day?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FOURTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TABLED
speechtext:
I assume that the assistant clerk will read the report as soon as it is noted, and it will appear in the Votes and Proceedings.
The Clerk Assistant then read the report, as follows:
Mr. Gordon, from the select committee appointed to investigate the Beauharnois project then presented the following as its fourth report:
1.	On the 10th day of June, 1931, the House of Commons adopted the following resolution: that Messrs. Dorion, Fiset (Sir Eugene), Gardiner, Gordon, Jacobs, Jones, Lennox, Mackenzie (Vancouver Centre), Stewart (Lethbridge), be a committee to investigate from its inception the Beauharnois project for the development of hydro-electric energy by the use of the waters of the St. Lawrence river so far as the matters referred to are within the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, and without restricting the generality of the foregoing words in particular to investigate the matters referred to in the speech made in the House of Commons by Mr. Robert Gardiner, the honourable member for Acadia, on the 10th day of May last, as reported on pages 18751887 of Hansard, and to report from time to time their observations and opinion thereon; with power to send for papers, persons and records. Hon, W. A. Gordon was on the 15th of June, 1931, appointed chairman of the special select committee.
2.	(1) The committee sat from the 15th day of June, 1931, to the 22nd day of July, 1931, held on most of these days more than one session and examined 35 witnesses.
(2)	On the 1st of July, the members of the committee visited and inspected the site of the works.	,
There were filed with .the committee 129 exhibits.
3.	Sonianges Section

St. Lawrence River
(1)	The Soulanges section of the St. Lawrence river is that portion thereof lying between Lake St. Francis and Lake St. Louis which are some 141 miles apart, and between which there is a fall of 83 feet. The average normal available flow of the river through this section is in the vicinity of 230,000 cubic feet ppr second for 50 per cent of the time making possible a development of 2,000,000 horse power of commercial electric energy at 85 per cent

Beauharnois Power-Report
load factor. The site is in close proximity to the city and port of Montreal, and is conveniently located on what must soon be a waterway capable of accommodating ocean-going vessels. It has therefore great possibility for industrial development if cheap power is available.
(2)	It is apparent that the Soulanges section thus presents an opportunity for hydro-electric development almost if not quite unique on the face of the globe. It is one of the greatest national resources in Canada, and in its natural state of great potential vaiue.
4.	History
(1)	About the year 1800, Edward Ellice, the Seigneur of Beauharnois, erected a small "moulin Banal" at the mouth of the St. Louis river and in order to increase the flow of the river, in 1807 built a small feeder, four miles in length, from Lake St. Francis to the head waters of the river. This constituted the first diversion in the Soulanges section of the St. Lawrence river for power purposes. Whatever water rights were incidental to this feeder later passed into the hands of a family named Robert and apparently formed the basis of the applications for power rights hereinafter mentioned. Details concerning the Robert "rights" may be found in a judgment delivered in the Exchequer Court of Canada in the case of Robert vs. the King (9 Exchequer Court Reports). Reference may be had also to Exhibit No. 29. a memorandum prepared by Mr. R. C. Alexander.
(2)	in 1855 the government of the province of Canada built a dyke, known as the Hungry Bay Dylce, as a protection against floods. It rebuilt the control gates of the feeder and in 1883 the government of Canada deepened and widened the feeder and installed new gates in the dyke at the feeder entrance, considerable sums of money having been appropriated for this purpose.
(3)	In 1902, J. B. Robert, as the grantee of the representatives of Edward Ellice, brought action against the crown for a declaration of his rights and judgment was pronounced on the 17th October. 1904. deciding that Robert held substantial rights in the feeder. A compromise was arrived at by which tne feeder was leased to the heirs of ,T. B. Robert by the Department of Public Works under date of the 28tli December. 1909, for a period of 21 years. This was authorized by order in council, P.C. 2168, of the 9th December. 1909.
14) Tn 1902 by Quebec Statute 2 Edward VII. Chapter 72 of the 2fitli March, 1902, the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company was incorporated with power to enlarge and extend the feeder. As a consequence of the finding of the Exchequer Court that J. B. Robert was not the owner of the feeder, in 1910 another Provincial Act was passed giving the Company the right to build a new canal or feeder from any point on the original feeder to any point on the St. Louis River at or near the town of Beauharnois. This Company thus became possessed of certain rights in respect of the diversion of rvater for power purposes from lake St. Francis. The shares of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company were all owned by W. H. Robert and other members of the Robert family. On the 3rd February, 1927, Mr. R. O. Sweezey obtained
from the Roberts an option of all the issued capital stock of the Company and the Company's rights.
The Robert interests
(5)	W. H. Robert and the other Robert heirs received for the 2,000 shares of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company and such other rights, if any, as were then outstanding in them
(1)	Cash $1,520,000.
(2)	200 fully paid part interests in the Beauharnois Power Syndicate.
(3)	21,000 class A shares of the Beauharnois Power Corporation.
(4)	100 fully paid part interests in the Beauharnois Syndicate transferred from R. O. Sweezey account, which became 200 part interests in the Beauharnois Power Syndicate.
(6)	In addition to the above-mentioned 400 part interests in the Power Syndicate owned by the Roberts, W. H. Robert held a further 300 units in his own name on which he owed $10,000 as at December 17th, 1929. For the 700 part interests, referred to above, the Robert heirs received, on the dissolution of the Syndicate, cheques aggregating $95,000, together with 28.000 shares of the class A common stock of the Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited.
(7)	In the same year, Mr. Sweezey applied to the Quebec Legislature for an amendment to the Act incorporating the Company permitting the construction of a canal between lake St. Francis and lake St. Louis. This application was refused.
(8)	On the 17th March, 1927, the Beauharnois Light. Heat and Power Company applied to His Excellency the Governor General in Council for approval of a proposal to build a power canal "which can be readily adapted for thirty foot navigation requirements also" from a point on lake St. Francis near the mouth of the St. Louis feeder to lake St. Louis and to use so much of the water of the St. Lawrence river as can be taken through the proposed canal without interfering with navigation and without interfering with existing prior rights in the river St. Lawrence." This application was not pressed.
(9)	On the 17th January, 1928, the Beauharnois Light. Heat and Power Company applied to His Excellency the Governor General in Council "for approval under the Navigable Waters Protection Act of its plans and site of proposed works herein described and for the right to divert forty thousand cubic feet per second (40,900 c.f.s.) from lake St. Francis."
(10)	In March, 1928, by Statute of the province of Quebec (18 George V, Chapter 113), a new section, 11A, was added to the original Act of incorporation giving the Company the right to build a new canal from any point within two miles in a southwesterly direction from the mouth of the St. Louis feeder to any point on lake St. Louis within one and a half miles in a westerly direction along the shore of lake St. Louis from the mouth of the St. Louis river and giving the Company the right to expropriate lands not exceeding six arpents in width.
(11)	On the 27th April, 1928, Mr. Sweezey and his associates obtained the passing of an order in council by the executive council of Quebec authorizing the granting to the Beauharnois Light. Heat and Power Company of an emphyteutic lease, which lease was subse-

quently executed on the 23rd June, 1928, and which grants to the Beauhornois Light, Heat and Power Company the rights of the province of Quebec to such part of the hydraulic power of the St. Lawrence River as can be developed between Lake St. Francis and Lake St. Louis through a derivation (six diversion) canal on the right (southern) shore of a maximum flowing capacity of forty thousand cubic feet per second (40,000 c.f.s.), (the province reserving the ownership and the free disposition of the surplus) for a period of 75 years from the 23rd June, 1928, at an annual rental of $20,000 for the first five years and $50,000 for each of the subsequent years and an additional payment of $1 for each horse power year revisable after each period of ten years from the date the plant will have been put in operation. 7.	Hungry -Bay Dyke
(1)	The province of Canada in 1856 and subsequent year, constructed a dyke along the shore of that part of lake St. Francis known as Hungry bay. This dyke at Confederation passed to the control of the Dominion of Canada, and it has since been maintained through the agency of the Federal Department of Railways and Canals. It will be necessary before water can be diverted to the canal from lake St. Francis that permission be obtained from the crown in the right of the Dominion of Canada to breach this dyke.
(2)	An application was made on the 29th day of July, 1929, for a conveyance to the company of that part of the dyke opposite the lands ow-ned by the Beauharnois Company, to the extent of 9,064 feet measured along the dyke. This application is now pending.
8.	Ambiguity in Order in Council
(1)	Condition number 3 of order in council
P.C. 522 provides that "the diversion of water shall not at any time exceed the maximum quantity of 40,000 cubic feet per second." If this means that at no time can the quantity of water diverted exceed 40,000 eubic feet per second, it is doubtful whether 500,000 h.p. can be developed by the use of that quantity of water, even adding thereto the 13,072 cubic second feet obtained by assignment of the Montreal Cotton Company's lease.
(2)	Your committee is of the opinion that any ambiguity in this respect should be removed.
9.	Control of Water
(1) The present plans do not provide for the control of the water at the entrance to the proposed canal. It has been stated in evidence that for this purpose and for reasons of safety, some method of control should be adopted, whether by way of a dam and gates, or a control lock at this point.
(2)	Considerable time was spent by Mr. Henry in an endeavour to establish that proper control could be maintained by the Dominion authorities at the gates leading to the water wheels.
(3)	Your committee was impressed with the idea that there should be some means of control at the entrance to the canal.
10.	Site of Works
(1)	The topography of the locality and the ground at the site of the works are of such
a character as to render possible and of comparatively easy attainment the large power development contemplated at a quite reasonable cost.
(2)	Your committee is of the opinion that from the physical standpoint a power development on the south shore of the Soulanges section of the St. Lawrence river is fundamentally sound and that with proper safeguards and regulation a navigable canal can be developed synchronously with the power develop-and utilized as a link in the St. Lawrence great waterway, at a reasonable cost to the Dominion of Canada for locks and bridges.
(3)	While the present plans are not in accordance with the proposals of the International Joint Board for this section of the river mentioned in their report of 1926, nevertheless, in view of the amount of money already expended, and of the possibility, as we believe, of the utilization of this canal for navigation purposes, we think that from the navigation standpoint the scheme should not be abandoned.

Shall the item carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. I feel strongly on this question. Naturally I would because I think it was under our administration that this grant to the horticultural council was first introduced. Reference has oeen made to lobbying around the buildings. My recollection is that the horticultural council's system of lobbying consisted of this: By appointment they met members. of the government in the railway committee room on a certain day; they met the former Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) the late Mr. Robb, the former Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler), your humble servant, and two or three other members of the government. Mr. Burrows, the secretary of the council, was there leading the horticultural interests with a large body of representative men from all over Canada. They must have been there at least an hour and a quarter making out their case before the government. Was there anything wrong in that? Nothing could have been more upright, nothing more honourable and fair. It is true Mr. Burrows made out as good a case as he could, but is that not what the council employed him for? I do not know that, from his standpoint, he went any further than he should, but I ha\e

no doubt that he touched the low tariff susceptibilities of some of the people who listened to him. The very fact that both governments gave some consideration to those representations is an evidence that they were pedalling along the right lines, as I see it, and consequently they were not doing anything dishonourable or wrong at that time in making the .representations they did make in connection with the tariff.
I would much rather be supporting my hon. friends who hold the opposite view than be supporting the ministry, but on the other hand I am not going to refuse to support the ministry when their course is identical with the course I took a year ago.

The explanation of the system of lobbying carried on by this body, as given by the hon. member for Melville, is not correct. It is true that this man Burrows, the secretary of that council, organized a deputation from all over Canada, which came to the government and presented its views in the railway committee room of this house, but what the hon. member for Melville does not know is that an active lobby was conducted in the corridors of this building in connection with individual members. Of course the ex-minister was not lobbied; they knew where he stood. It was those who took the other view who were lobbied. I know that to be so, and this man Burrows admitted it when I accused him. More than that, he openly boasted in this city that he hoped the United States would raise their tariff against us, because he said that was the only thing that would force the Liberal government to raise the tariff against the United States.

I should like to come back to the question with which I was dealing a few moments ago; I refer to the questions of cold storage and pre-cooling. In the part of Canada which I have the honour to represent the pre-cooling of fruit before it is sent to the market is receiving a great deal of attention, and I should like the minister tc say in a few words what the policy of his department is to be on the question of precooling and cold storage grants. I understood, from his answers a few moments ago, that during the present fiscal year the government does not propose to make any advances . except under the Cold Storage Act, and that all the advances in the list given were under that act. I should like to ba quite sure of that, because I understood that certain advances of government money were made, not under the act but by the department under some policy of its own, to certain applicants in certain parts of Canada. I know the matter has been before the minister and that he has given it a great deal of attention, and I should like him to say a few words to the committee-for the benefit of my constituents, I will admit, because I want them to know the policy of the government -as to what he intends to do in this matter of grants for pre-cooling and cold storage equipment for fruit particularly.

The policy of the government is to give assistance, under the Cold Storage Act, to cold storage plants fruit and otherwise, which are open to receive public storage or which are operated by cooperative associations. All the grants we are making this year are under the Cold Storage Act, and as yet we have not received sufficient applications to take up the whole amount.

Might I ask
the percentage of the grant?

It is 15 per cent
the first year, 7 per cent the second year, 4 per cent the third year and 2 per cent the fourth year.
Which amounts to about 30 per cent in all?
Yes, roughly.

I think that brings out the information desired by my hon. friend from Hants-Kings. Under the Cold Storage Act the grants are governed by statute, and the money7 must be paid out as my hon. friend has indicated. In addition to that, however, under the old government we had a distinct policy which came under what we called the pre-cooling vote. Under that vote a grant was given amounting to practically the same percentage as the cold storage grant, but it was all paid at once. It makes a great deal of difference to the fruit men whether they get the money all at once or whether it is spread over three or four years. I know the vote was not large but it met a very urgent necessity, especially in those districts which were heavily in debt in connection with the construction of large packing plants. That was particularly so in the Okanagan valley some ten or twelve years ago. They got their money grant under this pre-ccoling vote all at once and equipped their packing plants with modem pre-cooling equipment beginning about the year 1923- the first of their kind in Canada.

I think my hon. friend the minister is making a mistake in departing from that policy. We usually had that vote included in the supplementary estimates, amounting to from $20,000 to $40,000. I see a long and very formidable looking list of individual payments in the supplementary estimates in connection with animals slaughtered outside the provisions of the Health of Animals Act, but they do not total very much. A vote of $40,000 or $50,000 would have meant a great deal in the establishment of pre-cooling plants in the various fruit districts of Canada. The supplementary estimates have been brought down, but we have heard of further supplementary estimates, and if the minister can get in his digs I would suggest that he include an item of about $30,000 for pre-cooling plants such as were suggested by the hon. member for Hants-Kings.

Item agreed to.
For experiments in dehydration of fruits and vegetables, $20,000.

I should like to know
what progress they are making with these experiments in the dehydration of fruits and vegetables.

Experiments are
being carried on in Nova Scotia with the view of developing an apple cider free from the objections raised to apple cider in the past. It is hoped in that way to develop a market for the apples of Nova Scotia and to help the people learn the best apple for this particular use. We have there an arrangement with one of the cider pressing plants under which we carry on the experiments and provide the chemicals and some of the apparatus. The company does the bottling, buys the apples and puts the goods on the market. In Ontario We are carrying on somewhat similar work at Oakville and other plaices. In British Columbia also work is being done in connection with apricots, primes and so on, because we feel that while we have a market now for practically all those fruits produced in British Columbia, since large numbers of young orchards have been planted which will be bearing fruit in the near future, we must do all we can to put these people in a position to market their products through another channel and thus compete with outside interests.

Item agreed to.
